description: British delta-wing strategic bomber of the RAF V-force; one of few Vulcans preserved in the United States.
Canadian all-weather interceptor, the only fighter of wholly Canadian design to enter mass production.
Military version of the Beech Model 18, used for light transport, navigation and bombardier training.
Prototype service-test example of the T-34 Mentor piston trainer, derived from the Bonanza.
Twin-engine Marine Corps attack helicopter, the definitive Cobra gunship of the post-Vietnam era.
Early American air-launched strategic stand-off missile, carried by the B-47; cancelled in 1958.
The definitive utility helicopter of the Vietnam War, universally known as the Huey.
Bubble-canopy light helicopter widely used for observation and medical evacuation; the MASH helicopter.
Four-engine heavy bomber of the daylight strategic bombing campaign over Europe.
Pressurised very-long-range heavy bomber built for the Pacific war; the most advanced bomber of WWII.
Swept-wing six-jet medium bomber that set the template for all later jet aircraft design.
Tandem-rotor heavy-lift transport helicopter, in Army service since the early 1960s.
Carrier-capable multirole fighter finished in the markings of the Navy flight demonstration squadron.
Four-engine jet aerial refuelling tanker that made global strategic air power routine.
Piston-engine tanker-transport derived from the B-50, fitted with auxiliary jet pods in the L model.
Weather-reconnaissance conversion of the B-50, flown on long-range atmospheric sampling missions.
Push-pull twin used for forward air control and psychological-operations work over Vietnam.
Two-seat light trainer, one of the most widely produced civil aircraft in history.
Side-by-side primary jet trainer, nicknamed for the shrill whistle of its engines.
Military version of the Cessna 310 used for light staff transport and liaison duties.
Wood-and-fabric twin-engine advanced trainer, known to its crews as the Bamboo Bomber.
Long-range heavy bomber built in greater numbers than any other American aircraft of WWII.
First operational supersonic strategic bomber, capable of Mach 2 with an underslung weapons pod.
Delta-wing interceptor, the first aircraft designed around the area rule for transonic drag.
Ultimate American dedicated interceptor, guarding North American airspace into the 1980s.
Twin-engine search and rescue transport derived from the Convair 240 airliner.
Ten-engine strategic reconnaissance bomber; the largest piston-engine combat aircraft ever built.
Large twin-engine transport best known for flying the Hump over the Himalayas to China.
Rugged short-takeoff utility aircraft, later redesignated U-6, prized for bush operations.
Fast twin-engine attack bomber that saw combat in the Second World War, Korea and Vietnam.
Compact carrier-based light attack jet designed by Ed Heinemann, nicknamed the Scooter.
DC-2-derived medium bomber, the Army's standard bomber immediately before WWII; very few survive.
Improved development of the B-18 and the first American bomber with a tail gun position; 38 built.
Military DC-3; the workhorse transport of every Allied theatre, from D-Day to the Berlin Airlift.
Navy designation for the four-engine C-54 Skymaster long-range transport.
Reconnaissance conversion of the largest aircraft ever operated routinely from carrier decks.
Carrier dive bomber that sank four Japanese carriers at Midway and turned the Pacific war.
Twin-boom cargo aircraft built for paratroop and vehicle airdrop.
Assault transport for short unpaved strips; K models added auxiliary jet pods for hot-and-high work.
Open-cockpit radial-engine primary trainer used to screen wartime pilot candidates.
Lightweight fly-by-wire multirole fighter; the most widely exported Western fighter of its era.
Strategic bomber version of the swing-wing F-111, flown by Strategic Air Command.
All-weather carrier attack aircraft able to strike in darkness and bad weather with radar bombing.
Swing-wing carrier fleet defence fighter; the D was the final and most capable Tomcat variant.
Amphibious search and rescue flying boat that recovered downed aircrew at sea.
Carrier-based anti-submarine aircraft combining hunter and killer roles in one airframe.
Intermeshing-rotor crash rescue helicopter, stationed at airfields for immediate fire response.
Japanese-built target drone, also designated Q-19A, used for gunnery and missile practice.
Military version of the Model 18 Lodestar airliner, used for staff and light cargo transport.
Airborne early warning conversion of the Constellation, carrying radar in dorsal and ventral radomes.
Two-seat version of the razor-winged Mach 2 interceptor known as the missile with a man in it.
First American jet fighter to enter operational service and to score a jet-versus-jet kill.
All-weather radar-equipped interceptor developed from the T-33 trainer.
Special operations Hercules configured for covert refuelling of helicopters at night.
Two-seat jet trainer derived from the F-80; trained a generation of Western jet pilots.
Electronic warfare version of the American-built Canberra, flown to test air defence networks.
Air-launched decoy carried by the B-52 to mimic the bomber's radar signature and saturate defences.
Vertical and short takeoff attack jet flown by the Marine Corps from small decks and forward sites.
Twin-engine air superiority fighter designed for undisputed control of the air.
Presidential and vice-presidential transport that served as Air Force One and Air Force Two; open for tours.
Two-seat long-range interceptor armed with unguided nuclear-tipped air-to-air rockets.
Definitive Cold War multirole fighter, displayed in the markings of the Air Force demonstration team.
Final Navy Phantom variant, upgraded with leading-edge slats and strengthened airframe.
Soviet supersonic interceptor produced in greater numbers than any other jet fighter.
Training shape of the Mk.17 thermonuclear bomb, among the largest and heaviest US weapons ever fielded.
Remotely piloted lifting-body research vehicle flown once at Dryden to study low-speed lifting-body handling.
Canadian-built Harvard, the Commonwealth counterpart of the AT-6 Texan advanced trainer.
Supersonic air-launched stand-off nuclear cruise missile carried in pairs under the B-52.
Medium bomber made famous by the 1942 Doolittle raid launched from the carrier Hornet.
First operational American four-engine jet bomber and the first to drop a nuclear weapon from a jet.
First American fighter capable of supersonic speed in level flight; heavily used over Vietnam.
Swept-wing fighter of Korean War fame; the H was a fighter-bomber variant with a deeper fuselage.
Fast carrier-based reconnaissance aircraft, originally designed as a supersonic nuclear bomber.
Swept-wing utility jet used for combat readiness training and rapid staff transport.
All-weather interceptor; the J model carried the unguided nuclear Genie air-to-air rocket.
First supersonic trainer in the world, still the Air Force's advanced jet trainer.
Four-seat carrier-based electronic attack aircraft that jammed enemy radar and communications.
Militarised Piper Cub used for artillery spotting, liaison and courier work.
Large supersonic fighter-bomber built around an internal bomb bay for nuclear strike.
Straight-wing early jet fighter-bomber, the Air Force's first aircraft to refuel in flight operationally.
Swept-wing development of the Thunderjet with substantially improved performance.
Jet-powered target drone, later adapted for unmanned reconnaissance over hostile territory.
Open-cockpit monoplane primary trainer with a distinctive exposed radial engine.
Two-seat trainer version of the Swedish double-delta Draken, in Royal Danish Air Force markings.
Training glider used to teach the fundamentals of soaring flight to wartime glider pilots.
Navy shipboard helicopter for anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare, based on the Black Hawk.
Liaison and observation aircraft used for artillery spotting and casualty evacuation.
Photo-reconnaissance Crusader; flew the low-level runs that documented missiles in Cuba in 1962.
Basic trainer flown between primary and advanced training, nicknamed the Vultee Vibrator.
Stealth attack aircraft and Desert Storm combat veteran; arrived from Tonopah in July 2022 and is being prepared for display.
Torpedo bomber recovered after ditching off Daytona Beach in 2022; received by the museum in May 2024.
Early light helicopter donated to the museum in December 2023.
